title: Booked to Wait
passage:
The mate on the first sailing has taken to carrying a paperback. He reads it at the Brackenhithe slip with the ramp down and the engines turning, because the boat is now booked to sit there. In 2005 the crossing to the north shore was printed as eighteen minutes. This year it is printed as twenty-seven. The water is the same width it always was. Since 2011 the operator has earned a quality payment in any quarter when at least ninety-two per cent of its sailings berth within ten minutes of the booked minute, and has taken it in twenty-three of the last twenty-four quarters. The published reliability figure stood at seventy-one per cent in 2005. Last year it was ninety-six. By the only measure the contract knows, the crossing has never run better.

Kathleen Cattermay, a transport analyst working on contract, was asked by the county’s scrutiny committee for something narrow. She went at it from the passenger’s end. Every ticketed vehicle at Brackenhithe is stamped twice, at the barrier on the slip and at the ramp on the far side. She has those stamps going back to 2012. The median time from barrier to far ramp has gone from thirty-nine minutes to fifty-four. The booked crossing sets the length of a round trip, the round trip sets how many departures fit into a day, and a passenger waits for a departure, not a boat. Add nine minutes at each end and you lose a sailing, and the lost sailing costs everyone not on it far more than the nine minutes cost the boat. “The fifteen minutes are real, and I’d stand behind them in any room,” she says. “Ask me how many of them the timetable put there and I’ll give you a range, not a number. Something else happened in the middle of my series that I can’t take apart yet.”

Trevor Cottam has run operations for the company for eleven years and says the something else is nearly the whole of it. He starts with 2005. The median crossing that year took twenty-four minutes against an eighteen-minute booking. In his reading the old seventy-one per cent measured a promise nobody could keep, and six of the nine added minutes only brought the book level with the boat. Then there is work that really has got longer. The linkspan – the hinged ramp the vehicles drive over – was rebuilt in 2013 for heavier axle loads, and its locking sequence takes a manufacturer’s ninety seconds at each berth. And in 2016 the relief boat’s passenger certificate ran out and the company did not replace her. “Two boats and the old book gave you a departure every twenty-five minutes,” Cottam says. “One boat gives you one every seventy. Pad the book by nothing at all and you’d still have that.”

Alison Bexwarden drafted the punctuality clause for the transport authority in 2011 and does not accept that it caused any of this. In the consultation that preceded it, sixty-one per cent of those answering ranked getting across sooner below knowing when the boat would go. The clause measures what people asked to have measured. She will concede the shape of the incentive: an operator publishes a year ahead and is penalised for altering the book inside a year, so a contract of that shape produces a cautious book. What she volunteers is something nobody asks her about. A sailing that does not run is not late; it leaves the count altogether. In the first quarter of 2023 the crossing lost forty-one sailings to weather and a gearbox, and its reliability figure was ninety-seven per cent, the highest it had ever been. “That’s the line I’d change,” she says, “and nobody writes to me about it.”

Nobody disputes the stamps. Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing, and does not contest the fifteen minutes. Where Cattermay’s case thins is the join. Her thirteen years hold the linkspan work, the padding and the loss of the relief boat, and she says herself that she cannot pull them apart. The timetable is the reading she prefers; the stamps would bear either of the other two just as well. Cottam’s account has a soft place in the same decade. The book went from eighteen minutes to twenty-four in 2013, three years before the certificate ran out, and the interval between departures went from twenty-five minutes to thirty-two. Some of the frequency was gone before the boat was. The ninety seconds is a manufacturer’s figure; nobody has timed it on the linkspan. None of the three is arguing about the sentence Bexwarden raised herself. The service goes out to tender in the spring. The draft that went to the harbour board in July carries the 2011 clause word for word, including the line about cancelled sailings.
– Julian Dowlesham

questions.prompt: What are we told about the quality payment in the operator’s contract?

options.text: It turns on how far behind the booked minute the average sailing berths.
It was written into the contract when the second boat was withdrawn.
It has gone unpaid in one quarter during the past six years.
It is reduced, though not withdrawn, in quarters when sailings are cancelled.

questions.rationale: KEY C. Paragraph 1 gives the record: the operator has taken the quality payment in twenty-three of the last twenty-four quarters. C restates that from the other end – one quarter unpaid in six years – without reusing the passage’s figures in the passage’s order. A is a WRONG-MECHANISM trap: the clause counts the share of sailings that berth within ten minutes of the booked minute, so a sailing forty minutes behind counts against the operator exactly as one eleven minutes behind does, and nothing in the payment turns on how far behind the average sailing is. Real regimes come in both shapes, so a reader who knows the field cannot settle A from outside the text. B is a WRONG-LOCATION splice: both facts are in the text (the clause dates from 2011, the relief boat went in 2016) but the text never joins them, and the five-year gap refutes the join. D is the OUTSIDE-KNOWLEDGE trap, and the strongest one here, because real performance regimes usually do dock an operator for cancellations; paragraph 4 says the opposite – a sailing that does not run leaves the count altogether, and the quarter that lost forty-one sailings posted the highest figure the crossing had ever had – so the payment is neither reduced nor withheld. D is also the most qualified-sounding option in the set (‘though not withdrawn’), which is deliberate: the hedge-picking heuristic lands on a distractor here, and no option in the set carries an absolute for the strip-the-absolutes heuristic to work on.

questions.prompt: What does Cottam say about the 2005 timetable?

options.text: It already allowed less time for the crossing than the boat was taking.
It had sailings leaving seventy minutes apart, as they still do.
It made no allowance for loading, which took longer then than it does now.
It was written before anyone was measuring how late the boat was.

questions.rationale: KEY A. In paragraph 3 Cottam’s first move is that the median crossing in 2005 took twenty-four minutes against an eighteen-minute booking, so the boat was already over the printed time before any minutes were added; A restates that in different words. B is a WRONG-PERIOD number swap: seventy minutes is the interval Cottam gives for one boat under the present book, and his figure for the old book with two boats is a departure every twenty-five minutes, so B hands the 2005 timetable a spacing it did not have – and the second half of the option, ‘as they still do’, matches his figure for today, which is what makes the first half easy to wave through. C is a DIRECTION-REVERSAL trap with no support, and it is the kind of thing an operator’s man might well say – the book allowed for the water but not for the ramps – which is why it is here; Cottam’s point about 2005 is the crossing itself, six minutes over the book, and his loading-time point is the linkspan, rebuilt in 2013 with a locking sequence he lists under work that has got longer – so loading takes longer now than it did then, and C’s relative clause runs the other way. D is a WRONG-LOCATION inference that a skimmer reaches by dating measurement to the 2011 clause; paragraph 1 gives a published reliability figure for 2005, so somebody was measuring six years earlier.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the withdrawal of the relief boat?

options.text: It came before the first minutes were put on the book.
It had more to do with the rebuilt linkspan than with the boat’s certificate.
It is what first began to stretch the gap between one departure and the next.
It removed more departures from the day than the timetable changes had.

questions.rationale: KEY D. This is a one-inch inference from arithmetic the text supplies but never adds up. Cottam says two boats and the old book gave a departure every twenty-five minutes and one boat gives one every seventy; paragraph 5 says the interval had already gone from twenty-five to thirty-two under the 2013 book, three years before the certificate ran out. So the timetable accounts for about seven minutes of that interval and the lost boat for about thirty-eight: losing the boat took more departures out of the day than the padding did. Every distractor is shaped as an inference too, so ‘pick the one that sounds inferred’ has nothing to work on. A is a WRONG-ORDER inference: the book went from eighteen to twenty-four minutes in 2013 and the certificate ran out in 2016, so six of the nine added minutes were on the book before the boat went. B is a WRONG-LOCATION splice of two neighbouring sentences: the linkspan rebuild and the certificate stand side by side in paragraph 3, but the text gives one cause for the withdrawal – the relief boat’s passenger certificate ran out and the company did not replace her – and says nothing that joins the ramp to the boat; paragraph 5 has two boats still running a thirty-two-minute interval for three years after the linkspan was rebuilt, so the ramp did not take the second boat off the run. C is the OVERGENERALISATION of Cottam’s position – the lost boat as the whole of where the frequency went – and paragraph 5 refutes it in terms: the interval had lengthened from twenty-five to thirty-two minutes before the boat was withdrawn, so some of the frequency was gone before the boat was and the withdrawal cannot be what first stretched the gap between departures.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude towards Cattermay’s argument?

options.text: He thinks her minutes show little and her explanation still less.
He accepts her numbers but not the cause she assigns them.
He takes her to have shown the timetable at fault, though not by how much.
He doubts her numbers but grants that the timetable is probably to blame.

questions.rationale: KEY B. Paragraph 5 is the writer’s verdict and it splits. On her measurement he is unreserved: nobody disputes the stamps, and Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing. On her explanation he is not: where her case thins is the join, her thirteen years hold the linkspan work, the padding and the loss of the relief boat together, she says herself that she cannot pull them apart, and the timetable is the reading she prefers while the stamps would bear either of the other two just as well. B states that division – her numbers stand, the cause she assigns them does not. A is the DISMISSIVE misread, both legs refused: it dies on the paragraph’s first three words, ‘Nobody disputes the stamps’, and again on what the writer does with her explanation, which he neither refutes nor ranks below the other two – ‘the stamps would bear either of the other two just as well’ is indifference between three readings, not a verdict against hers. C is the ROLE-OR-ATTRIBUTION SWAP that is this family’s signature, in its finer form: it is Cattermay’s own position, firm on the measurement and open on the share, handed to the writer, who goes further than she does and declines to grant the timetable any of the fifteen minutes as shown. D reverses the split and dies where A does, on ‘Nobody disputes the stamps’, before its second half can be weighed. All four options are two-part verdicts over the same two legs, her numbers and her cause, and they fill every combination – both granted (C), both refused (A), and the two splits (B and D) – so no leg is settled by a majority of the options, no pair is the only pair of contraries, no option is a stronger or weaker form of another, and none carries an absolute; neither ‘strip the extremes’ nor ‘take the balanced one’ isolates the key, and a reader has to know which half of her case the writer grants. The neutral-reporter option this question type usually carries has been left out on purpose – the writer judges both principals in paragraph 5 and names what none of the three is arguing about, so it was never a live reading, and after the last two long passages a student would have learned to discard it on sight.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: A crossing that is booked slower than it was and runs to time more often, and the passengers who were not consulted.
A reliability figure and a set of ticket stamps that tell different stories, and a dispute over which of them to believe.
The punctuality clause in the current contract, and the argument over whether it should go into the next one unchanged.
A ferry whose punctuality record has improved while its passengers’ journeys have lengthened, and the disagreement over what connects the two.

questions.rationale: KEY D. The whole-text shape is a punctuality record that has risen from seventy-one to ninety-six per cent while the median barrier-to-ramp time has risen from thirty-nine minutes to fifty-four, and a three-way argument about what joins those two movements – the padding, the rebuilt linkspan or the lost relief boat – which paragraph 5 leaves standing, with a soft place found in Cattermay’s case and in Cottam’s account. D names the two movements and the disagreement over the join, and stops there, which is what the text does. All four options are pitched at the whole piece rather than at one paragraph, all four are two-limb noun phrases of much the same length, and each of the three wrong ones pairs a limb the text supports with a limb the text refuses, so none of them can be discarded on its face. A is the UNCONSULTED-PUBLIC reading. Its first limb is sound: the crossing is booked at twenty-seven minutes against eighteen, and the published figure has gone from seventy-one to ninety-six. Its second limb is the grievance a reader supplies unprompted, because the piece quotes an analyst, an operations manager and the drafter of the clause, and no passenger at all. Paragraph 4 refuses that grievance in one sentence: a consultation preceded the 2011 clause; sixty-one per cent of those answering ranked getting across sooner below knowing when the boat would go; and Bexwarden’s defence of the clause is that it measures what people asked to have measured. Note what A does not do: it sets the two movements side by side without claiming that either produced the other, and that silence, rather than any difference of confidence, is what separates it from D. B is the WRONG-OBJECT reading and the nearest miss. Its first limb is true in the plainest way, since the reliability figure tells one story about the crossing and the ticket stamps tell another, and that contrast is where the piece begins. Its second limb is what the text refuses. Paragraph 5 opens ‘Nobody disputes the stamps’; Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing and does not contest the fifteen minutes; and Cattermay’s ‘I’ll give you a range, not a number’, which is the line that baits this option, hedges where the minutes came from rather than whether they are there – she says in the same breath that they are real and that she would stand behind them in any room. Neither record is in doubt; what is argued about is what connects them. C is the CODA-AS-THESIS reading. It takes the last two sentences of the piece – the spring tender, and the July draft that carries the 2011 clause word for word – and makes the renewal of that clause the argument the text is having. The text is having no such argument. Bexwarden alone would change a line, and by her own account nobody writes to her about that line, while paragraph 5 says in terms that none of the three is arguing about the sentence she raised herself. The clause going forward unchanged is where the text stops, not what it is about.

repair_log.structural_finding: MAIN-IDEA COHERENCE FLOOR, for the owner package. Three rounds of repair on this one question have now closed three distinct blind channels - altitude (round 1: only the key sat at whole-text level), the A/D minimal pair (round 3: one option was the key with the causal join asserted rather than left open), and B's face-invalid first limb - and the blind solve rate has fallen from about 90 per cent (G-STEM r1) through 60 (r2) and 65 (r3) to about 40 per cent measured here. It has not fallen further, and the residual is not a defect that a fourth rebuild would remove. The key of a main-idea question is by definition a faithful summary of the whole text; the other four questions are by definition made out of parts of that same text; so on any well-built sheet the main-idea key is the option whose elements are most often named or implied by the rest of the sheet, and a solver who reasons 'the main idea is the option the other questions are made of' will be right more often than chance. Suppressing that would mean either making the key a WORSE summary than a distractor, or building detail questions that avoid the text's main material - both of which cost more, pedagogically, than the residual does. batch19's ELF long hit the same wall on its own main-idea question. The recommendation for the owner is therefore a policy one, not a repair one: either accept a disclosed ~2-in-5 floor on ELF main-idea items over multi-voice texts, or drop the main-idea family from long passages that carry four detail questions. This unit is shipped with the floor measured and disclosed, not papered over.
